title: Operator field journal — control plane provisioning, scaling experiments, and rotation recipes (WIP)
body:
Purpose:
This is a living operator journal for teams commissioning private control planes (VPC and on‑prem). The goal is to capture pragmatic, field‑tested recipes for first‑time installs, capacity growth experiments, scheduled rotations, and safe upgrades. Treat as a supplement to formal runbooks: shorter, operation‑centric notes, gotchas, and quick commands we actually use when heads‑down.

Audience:
Primary: platform operators and SREs running customer private control planes. Secondary: solutions and delivery engineers onboarding a customer (use these recipes to accelerate day‑one).

TL;DR (if you only scan):
- Start with a small, validated seed cluster (3 control nodes) with persistent etcd and colocated telemetry.
- Use the tf-patterns below to keep infra idempotent and testable locally via a kind/minikube harness.
- Autoscale via capacity classes (cpu/ram per slot) instead of bare GPU counts; route by policy to stable pools.
- Rotations: create a rotation ticket, evict pods, replace instance, validate health, then rotate next. No parallel rotations across >25% of a pool.
- Upgrades: always do control plane canaries in a staging replica using traffic mirroring and a short TTL fallback.

1) Quick checklist — initial provisioning (baseline cluster)
- Prep: Customer network topology diagram, CIDR blocks, peering/VPN creds, and KMS material.
- Seed control plane nodes: 3x VMs (baremetal: 3x dedicated hosts). OS: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, docker containerd stack pinned to known versions (see linked_artifacts for pins).
- Etcd: external cluster or dedicated disks with RAID‑1 for onprem. Use WAL rotation script from ops repo.
- Load balancer: HAProxy in front of API servers (health probe on /healthz).
- DNS: internal short TTL records for API endpoints; have an A record and a CNAME for canary endpoint.
- Storage: use hostPath CSI for small installs, move to Ceph/Rook for medium+ footprints.
- TLS: Issue control plane certs from customer CA or use ACM equivalent. Store certs in KMS and sync via the cert-syncer job.

2) Terraform module notes and patterns (practical)
- Module layout: keep 1 module per primitive (network, compute-pool, lb, kms-integration). Avoid a big "cp-bootstrap" that hides dependencies.
- Variables: prefer maps/lists over many booleans. Example pattern: compute_pools = [{name=\"cpu-stable\", instance_type=\"m5.xlarge\", min=2, max=8}, ...]. This makes autoscaling policy generation easier.
- State strategy: remote S3/Ceph object store with locking via Dynamo/Consul/DB. For onprem customers without S3, we use a local object store + postgres locker (module included).
- Versioning: tag tf module releases semantically and pin in customer manifests. Keep a changelog file with behavioral notes (breaking changes like renaming variable keys).
- Iterative apply: use terraform plan + -target for one resource when testing upgrades (example: -target=module.compute_pool[\"cpu-stable\"]). Avoid large concurrent changes.
- Testing harness: a lightweight kind cluster + local terraform provider for testing networking logic. Keep a tiny dataset for e2e smoke.

3) Scaling heuristics and experiments (what we learned)
- Batching small requests: throughput gains when increasing batch_size to 8 for non‑interactive jobs. For interactive chat workloads keep batch_size <= 2 to meet p95 latency SLOs.
- Autoscale triggers: prefer queue depth (requests/sec per worker) + GPU memory % rather than CPU utilization. Queue depth gives direct correlation to latency spikes.
- Pool sizing rule of thumb: start with capacity to handle 3x baseline qps for burst protection; fine tune to 1.5x after 72h of production metrics.
- Cold cache effect: first 10 minutes after a pool scale up show 15–30% higher latency due to KV cache warmup. Use warmup scripts for known hot prefixes.

4) Rotation recipe (day‑to‑day operator steps)
- Preconditions: create a rotation ticket in Jira, annotate with customer, pool, and safety window. Communicate on customer Slack channel.
- Step 1: mark node unschedulable: kubectl cordon NODE
- Step 2: gracefully evict: kubectl drain NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force --grace-period=120
- Step 3: monitor replication: ensure replacements reach Ready and health checks pass (api/metrics/kv).
- Step 4: replace instance through terraform: terraform apply -target=module.compute_pool.instance["NODE-ID"] (or equivalent host reprovision).
- Step 5: validate metrics for 10 min: p50/p95 latency, error rate, CPU/GPU util.
- Step 6: uncordon if healthy, close ticket.
- Rules: never rotate >1 node in a 3-node control plane at once. For large pools, limit concurrent rotations to 25% of pool size.

5) Upgrade plan (control plane and runtime)
- Stage: create staging control plane that mirrors prod config but small scale. Mirror 5–10% of traffic via traffic mirroring tools.
- Canary: upgrade control plane on staging, run smoke tests, then pick 1 compute pool in prod as canary (low qps pool).
- Rollout windows: prefer low‑traffic windows per customer (midnight local). For customers spanning timezones coordinate with their ops.
- Rollback path: have an explicit terraform rollback plan using pinned module version and stored tfstate snapshot. Snapshot tfstate before any major change.
- Post‑upgrade checks: reconcile admission webhooks, validate migrations, verify model artifacts load time within threshold.

6) Common failures + remediation (observed in the field)
- Etcd WAL corruption on abrupt power loss: remediation = restore from recent snapshot + reconfigure peer list; ensure WAL backup cadence increased to 5m for critical customers.
- API server 503s after config change: immediate step: check webhook timeouts (common culprit), then reduce concurrency or increase webhook timeout to 30s and retry.
- Strange kernel OOMs during large TF frontend builds: enforce mem limits on build hosts, move image builds to dedicated builders.
- TLS rotation flapping due to clock skew: ensure NTP is enforced on all hosts. If flapping, rotate cert TTL and force sync.

7) Observability and what to watch during ops
- Golden metrics: p95 latency, error_rate(5m), queue_depth, kv_hit_ratio, model_load_time, etcd_quorum_loss.
- Logs: watch for webhook timeout lines (~30s), node kubelet evictions, service account permission denies.
- Dashboards: have a single ops panel with red/amber/green thresholds for p95, error rate, and node health.

8) Quick commands & snippets (copyable)
- Cordoning + draining: kubectl cordon $NODE && kubectl drain $NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force --grace-period=120
- Reapply a compute pool: cd infra/terraform && terraform plan -target=module.compute_pool["cpu-stable"] && terraform apply -target=module.compute_pool["cpu-stable"]
- Snapshot tfstate: aws s3 cp s3://tfstate/customer-prod.tfstate ./snapshots/$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)-prod.tfstate
- Check etcd health: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://etcd-1:2379 endpoint health --cacert=/etc/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/etcd/etcd.crt --key=/etc/etcd/etcd.key

9) Postmortem template pointers (use when something goes wrong)
- Summary, timeline, impact, root cause, mitigation, action items with owners, verification plan. Keep <48h initial report cadence.

10) Open questions / TODOs
- Can we consolidate compute pool autoscaling triggers in a single operator vs per customer tf logic? Pros/cons and migration plan needed.
- Experiment: can we prepopulate KV cache during scale‑up using a gossip-based warmup instead of synchronous fetch? Run AB test in staging Q2.
- Add automated preflight terraform checks for list length changes that may trigger rolling replacements.

11) Links & references
- Terraform modules repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/tf-modules (see /modules/compute_pool)
- Upgrade checklist (formal): confluence:private-cp-upgrade-checklist-2025
- Ops scripts repo: github:https://github.com/redwood-inference/ops-scripts

Notes to self: keep this document short and pragmatic. After next successful rotation (2026-03) move stable patterns into the canonical runbook and simplify variable names. If any of the collaborators have additions, paste them below with the date.

-- Leah
